posts.name: Belle Sorciere
posts.cooked:
I find this one confusing. Relevant text quoted:

>

When a card enters play, the following order of things occurs.

  1. Ongoing effects on the card become applicable.
  2. Cards that react to other cards entering play now act.
  3. One-time effects on the card happen.

There is an exception to the order of operations ruling relating to reacting to damage being dealt. A card (or cards belonging to a hero/villain) that reacts to damage being dealt to it reacts before other cards do. The card dealing the damage and other interested cards happen afterwards and can be ordered by player choice.

Example: Suppose Mr. Fixer has Dual Crowbars and Bloody Knuckles in play. Omnitron has Adaptive Plating Subroutine but is not immune to anything yet. Mr. Fixer uses Strike to hit Omnitron for 3 melee damage. By this ruling, the text on Adaptive Plating Subroutine must go first and make Omnitron immune to melee damage. Then Dual Crowbars’ effect happens and Mr. Fixer can deal damage to another target. Without this ruling, you could use Synaptic Interruption and careful ordering to hit Omnitron twice before it becomes immune to melee damage.

The example sounds to me like adaptive plating subroutine effectively makes Omnitron immune to damage, and that doesn't seem correct. I assume I must be misreading something.

posts.name: AlexxKay
posts.cooked:
If a card is damaging the X lowest HP targets, and in the middle of doing that a new lowest HP target appears, the targeting does not change. The originally chosen X targets are damaged. If one disappears in the middle, the damage fizzles and does not re-target.

I would suggest rephrasing "the damage fizzles" to "the damage to the missing target fizzles".  We're talking about (often) multiple targets here, and any that *don't* disappear do still take damage, right?

 

1.    Ongoing effects on the card become applicable.
2.    Cards that react to other cards entering play now act.
3.    One-time effects on the card happen.

That strikes me as needlessly complex.  It would be much simpler to just make step 1 be "Text on the card takes effect." and have no step 3.  While one can easily construct an edge case where this makes a different outcome, I don't see any cases where it would cause an outcome that seems (to my intuition) wrong enough to make the added complexity worthwhile.

 

Expatriette’s Ammo cards can be played without a gun in play. If that happens, the Ammo card is destroyed.

I thought it went directly to the Trash, having never really entered play, and thus not triggering either "card enters play" or "card was destroyed" effects.  Has this changed?
 

If an ammo card is next to a gun card and the gun card is destroyed, the ammo card remains in play.

Uh, why?  Expatriette has enough trouble getting ammo cards out, so why make it so easy for one to end up in limbo?  She has many means of getting ammo out of her trash, but *none* for recovering an ammo card that gets detached like this.  It would make more sense to me to errata the ammo cards to say "If the Gun card this is next to is destroyed, so is this card."

Oh, wait.  Is there actually a situation that can destroy a gun instead of an ammo card that isn't due to players being perverse and/or dumb about their choice of resolving ambiguities?  I don't think there is.  Nevermind...
 

For the second instance of damage, Dual Crowbars is only restricted from selecting the target that was the final result of the first instance of damage (after all redirects).

Is this a general change to how targeting multiple targets works? I was under the impression that you couldn't re-choose the *initial* target, but you *could* re-choose a target that ended up getting damaged earlier due to redirects.  Is this still true in general, or not?

Just to cover an edge case here, if Fixed Point lets you get Jackhandle and Crowbars in play, your initialdamage would be changed to all target damage, and each Jackhandle hit would trigger Crowbars for that specific target and HP reduced.

Also, with redirection, say apostate's orb, a hit against the orb would cause you to be unable to target the Orb with the extra Crowbar hit, but if you targeted another relic it would still redirect to the Orb and damage it a second time.

My opposition to the new Crowbars is almost exclusively linked to my love of tough fights.  I get bored in fights that are stompfests, the matches where it feels like the heroes are competing to see who owns the hardest.

So I tend to dislike things that reward you for already doing awesomely, and prefer things that help you deal with nasty situations.

Dual Crowbar has never been my favorite tool, I like Hoist Chain and Tire Iron better.  Now Fixer has a Taiaha/Shockwave Hybrid, it works great, but it rewards you for stacking bonuses, and that isn't my cup of tea at all.

AlexxKay:
If a card is damaging the X lowest HP targets, and in the middle of doing that a new lowest HP target appears, the targeting does not change. The originally chosen X targets are damaged. If one disappears in the middle, the damage fizzles and does not re-target.
I would suggest rephrasing "the damage fizzles" to "the damage to the missing target fizzles".  We're talking about (often) multiple targets here, and any that *don't* disappear do still take damage, right? 

Yes, I can tweak the wording there.

1.    Ongoing effects on the card become applicable.2.    Cards that react to other cards entering play now act.3.    One-time effects on the card happen.  
That strikes me as needlessly complex.  It would be much simpler to just make step 1 be "Text on the card takes effect." and have no step 3.  While one can easily construct an edge case where this makes a different outcome, I don't see any cases where it would cause an outcome that seems (to my intuition) wrong enough to make the added complexity worthwhile. 

It's complex, but has to be that way or some weird things happen. It may not happen in tabletop play which is fine. We've learned that in the video game, if something weird can happen, it will happen to someone.

Expatriette’s Ammo cards can be played without a gun in play. If that happens, the Ammo card is destroyed.  
I thought it went directly to the Trash, having never really entered play, and thus not triggering either "card enters play" or "card was destroyed" effects.  Has this changed? 

I don't know if it has changed, I just know what it is.

If an ammo card is next to a gun card and the gun card is destroyed, the ammo card remains in play.  
Uh, why?  Expatriette has enough trouble getting ammo cards out, so why make it so easy for one to end up in limbo?  She has many means of getting ammo out of her trash, but *none* for recovering an ammo card that gets detached like this.  It would make more sense to me to errata the ammo cards to say "If the Gun card this is next to is destroyed, so is this card."Oh, wait.  Is there actually a situation that can destroy a gun instead of an ammo card that isn't due to players being perverse and/or dumb about their choice of resolving ambiguities?  I don't think there is.  Nevermind... 

Why = because Christopher said so.

For the second instance of damage, Dual Crowbars is only restricted from selecting the target that was the final result of the first instance of damage (after all redirects).  
Is this a general change to how targeting multiple targets works? I was under the impression that you couldn't re-choose the *initial* target, but you *could* re-choose a target that ended up getting damaged earlier due to redirects.  Is this still true in general, or not? 

No, it's not a change, just a clarification of Dual Crowbars in case anyone didn't know. Most of the things in the post are re-iterating existing clarifications, not changes. They are answers to questions we asked Christopher.
